seatMission: Design the offer, product, packaging and price.
seatResponsibilities: Design offer, product, packaging, pricing and product evidence.

criterionDimensions.name: Pricing science and willingness to pay

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I define the customer outcome the offer is intended to produce in observable terms rather than describing features as value.
I connect promised outcomes to a specific customer, context, job, and alternative instead of using generic benefit language.
I distinguish functional, economic, emotional, social, compliance, and risk-reduction value only where evidence supports the distinction.
I state value claims at a strength appropriate to available proof and avoid turning internal forecasts into customer promises.
I identify which outcomes are controlled by the product, jointly produced with the customer, or dependent on external conditions.
I distinguish immediate user value from buyer, operator, payer, and enterprise value when those roles differ.
I quantify value only with explicit assumptions, time horizon, baseline, and uncertainty.
I identify what customers must change or contribute for the promised outcome to be realistic.
I define invalidation conditions that would make the value proposition materially weaker or false.
I revise the outcome promise when field evidence shows that customers achieve different value than expected.
I distinguish a validated customer problem from a feature request, sales objection, executive idea, or technology capability.
I map product capabilities to customer jobs and outcomes so every material feature has a reason to exist.
I identify unmet, over-served, and adequately served needs rather than assuming more functionality always creates more value.
I test whether the intended customer can actually adopt, use, and realize value from the proposed offer.
I distinguish initial attraction from sustained usage, retention, and realized outcome evidence.
I identify customer segments where the same product requires materially different offers, onboarding, service, or economics.
I preserve evidence about non-users, churned users, failed pilots, and rejected offers as product-learning inputs.
I distinguish customer willingness to try from willingness to switch, pay, implement, and renew.
I identify dependencies on complementary products, integrations, skills, process changes, or third parties that affect fit.
I avoid declaring product-market or product-offer fit from isolated wins without repeatable behavioral and economic evidence.
I design offers as coherent combinations of outcome, scope, mechanism, deliverables, service, proof, terms, support, and risk rather than as feature bundles.
I define what is included, excluded, optional, and contingent so buyers and operators understand the real commitment.
I align offer components with the buyer's decision criteria and the operator's ability to deliver consistently.
I distinguish the core offer from bonuses, promotions, financing, guarantees, onboarding, and after-sale services.
I use guarantees and risk reversal only when obligations, exclusions, economics, and operational capacity are explicit.
I identify when service intensity is required to realize value and include that burden in the offer rather than hiding it.
I design proof into the offer through demonstrations, pilots, references, benchmarks, warranties, or measurable milestones appropriate to the claim.
I avoid adding components merely to make an offer appear larger when they increase confusion, cost, or delivery risk without material customer value.
I create materially distinct offer hypotheses when uncertainty remains instead of optimizing one favored design prematurely.
I version offer architecture as evidence, pricing, delivery capability, or customer needs change.
I prioritize product capabilities according to customer outcome, strategic differentiation, evidence, economics, risk, and dependency rather than stakeholder volume.
I distinguish must-have capability, differentiator, table stakes, experiment, convenience, and waste.
I identify the smallest coherent product scope capable of testing the decisive value hypothesis.
I resist shipping functionality that cannot be tied to a user task, customer outcome, regulatory requirement, operational need, or strategic option.
I consider reliability, usability, accessibility, security, privacy, supportability, and observability part of product scope rather than afterthoughts.
I make dependencies and sequencing explicit so roadmap priority reflects feasibility as well as desirability.
I identify features whose complexity or cost creates negative option value by making future change harder.
I use retirement and simplification as legitimate product decisions when evidence shows low value or disproportionate burden.
I distinguish roadmap commitments from hypotheses so uncertain items are not communicated as guaranteed delivery.
I revise priorities when realized usage, customer outcomes, economics, incidents, or market evidence contradict planned value.
I define differentiation in terms of customer-relevant outcomes, mechanisms, experience, economics, trust, or access rather than superficial uniqueness.
I distinguish a feature competitors lack today from a defensible advantage they cannot easily copy, neutralize, or bundle away.
I identify where parity is sufficient and differentiation spending would not materially change customer choice.
I connect product differentiation to target segments and use cases rather than assuming one advantage matters equally to every buyer.
I evaluate whether differentiation increases value enough to justify added complexity, cost, or switching burden.
I distinguish product differentiation from brand, channel, relationship, contractual, regulatory, and ecosystem advantages.
I anticipate likely competitor responses and avoid strategies that depend on rivals remaining static.
I use customer and win-loss evidence to test whether claimed differentiators actually influence choice.
I preserve multiple strategic product options when uncertainty is high and irreversible commitment is unnecessary.
I retire differentiation claims when evidence shows customers do not notice, value, believe, or pay for them.
I set pricing from customer value, willingness to pay, competitive alternatives, cost structure, strategic position, and evidence rather than cost-plus habit alone.
I distinguish list price, realized price, discount, concession, financing, rebate, and total customer cost.
I test willingness to pay with methods appropriate to the decision and do not treat hypothetical survey answers as equivalent to transactions.
I examine price sensitivity across segments, use cases, quantities, contract terms, and urgency states.
I identify reference prices, anchors, switching costs, procurement norms, and budget boundaries that shape customer response.
I connect price changes to volume, mix, retention, service burden, channel economics, and contribution rather than optimizing conversion alone.
I distinguish price experimentation from indiscriminate discounting and define learning objectives and stop conditions before testing.
I protect pricing claims and savings comparisons from unsupported assumptions or misleading baselines.
I model uncertainty and downside when price changes can materially affect cash, brand, channel relationships, or long-term retention.
I revise pricing when transaction evidence demonstrates that the existing value-capture logic is wrong.
I package capabilities so customers can understand what to buy, why one option fits them, and what changes across tiers.
I align packaging boundaries with meaningful differences in value, usage, service, risk, or customer segment rather than arbitrary feature withholding.
I avoid excessive plan complexity that increases decision friction, support burden, billing errors, or unintended customer behavior.
I define usage units and metering in terms customers and operators can understand and verify.
I evaluate subscription, perpetual, consumption, transaction, outcome-based, service, and hybrid models according to value realization and risk.
I connect contract length, renewal, cancellation, minimums, overages, and commitments to customer value and business economics.
I identify packaging that encourages harmful overuse, underuse, gaming, or cross-subsidy and redesign incentives when needed.
I design upgrade, downgrade, expansion, and migration paths that preserve customer agency and operational clarity.
I ensure taxes, fees, financing, refunds, guarantees, and exclusions are explicit before the customer commits.
I test packaging through customer comprehension, choice behavior, sales execution, delivery feasibility, and contribution economics.
I define the evidence required to validate product, offer, packaging, and pricing hypotheses before declaring them proven.
I use prototypes, concierge tests, pilots, controlled experiments, phased releases, and behavioral observation according to the uncertainty being reduced.
I distinguish usability success from value realization and conversion success from durable customer outcome.
I preserve null, negative, churn, refund, support, and incident evidence rather than measuring only positive engagement.
I define primary outcome, guardrails, target population, exposure, and decision rule before interpreting experiments.
I avoid claiming causal product impact from pre-post changes when major confounding changes remain uncontrolled.
I use qualitative evidence to understand mechanisms and quantitative evidence to estimate magnitude without forcing either beyond its scope.
I test transfer across materially different customers or contexts before generalizing a successful pilot.
I record product versions and treatment details so evidence remains attached to the product that actually generated it.
I stop or redesign experiments when harm, invalid measurement, implementation failure, or insufficient decision value makes continued testing unjustified.
I evaluate whether a capability should be built, bought, partnered, configured, reused, deferred, or killed based on strategic value and total lifecycle economics.
I include integration, migration, vendor dependence, security, privacy, reliability, support, talent, and exit costs in sourcing decisions.
I distinguish strategic core capabilities from commodity capabilities where custom development creates little customer advantage.
I evaluate product portfolio overlap, cannibalization, cross-sell, shared capabilities, and customer confusion before adding another offering.
I identify products or features that consume scarce capacity without sufficient strategic, customer, or economic return.
I use kill decisions to release capital and complexity rather than preserving low-value work because of sunk cost.
I preserve fallback and exit options when vendors, platforms, standards, or regulations create material dependency risk.
I avoid partner decisions based solely on brand prestige and assess concrete capability, incentives, economics, control, and accountability.
I sequence product investments according to dependencies and option value rather than treating every roadmap item as independently attractive.
I document why a portfolio decision was made so future teams can distinguish changed evidence from repeated historical debate.
I connect product decisions to contribution margin, cash timing, capacity, service cost, retention, risk, and enterprise value rather than revenue alone.
I maintain a roadmap that represents strategic choices, evidence gaps, dependencies, and learning milestones rather than a wish list of dates.
I distinguish committed delivery from discovery and preserve explicit decision gates between them.
I assign owners and measurable success conditions to major product and offer decisions.
I identify when growth in usage or customers would exceed operational, technical, support, compliance, or financial capacity.
I include deprecation, migration, support, incident response, and lifecycle cost in product governance.
I use leading indicators carefully and require realized customer and economic outcomes before declaring success.
I maintain traceability from roadmap items to customer evidence, strategic rationale, expected value, and decision owner.
I surface conflicts among customer value, short-term revenue, long-term architecture, legal constraints, ethics, and operational feasibility rather than hiding them in prioritization scores.
I consider an offer or product decision ready only when outcome, scope, price, evidence, economics, delivery feasibility, risks, and invalidation conditions are explicit.
